The HOLC area-description sheet for the polygon currently centered on screen slides up, and the grades flood back onto the map in the archival green, blue, yellow, and red, each grade paired with the surveyor's verbatim language from the digitized sheets. The FHA underwriting sentence prints beneath. The visitor now re-reads the cold-open map as a weapon. The act closes with the Supreme Court current rebuilt as a stepped sticky scene, two lanes and four gates (Buchanan, Corrigan, Hansberry, Shelley); the gates open while the hatching on the ground stays put, showing law voided on paper and intact in practice.

arc.act: Act VI. Public Money Moves the Ground
arc.chapters: Chapters 10-12 (The university rebuilds, The color tax, The Contract Buyers League)
arc.onScreen: Urban renewal is rendered as erasure. An aerial archival photograph crossfades with the ground plane, and as the visitor scrolls, cleared parcels blank out zone by zone while a counter fills toward 638 buildings and about 4,000 families, each figure sourced on screen. The blanked parcels stay blank for the rest of the page. Then the Two Buyers scene, sticky and split. Two identical house elevations side by side; each scrolled year from 1948 to 1968 drops a payment stub under both. The mortgage side accrues equity shading, the contract side stacks stubs at nearly double the price with the forfeiture clause visible, and the scene resolves on the $71,000 average overpayment with its source line. The CBL chapter answers it with the church-basement photograph, Ruth Wells and Clyde Ross verbatim, the payment strike shown as withheld stubs, and the first reversal entry printing into the ledger strip.

arc.act: Act VII. The Ledger and Your Feet
arc.chapters: Chapter 13 (The ledger and the ground today)
arc.onScreen: The ledger strip that has accumulated along the bottom since 1833 expands to fill the screen as one readable account of dollars and people across eleven entries. Then the true-scale climb. The Black median family wealth column, $44,890, passes in one short scroll. The white column, $285,010, takes 6.35 times the scroll distance, with era milestones marked along the way. The visitor's own thumb performs the measurement. Then the ground plane returns in present-day form with an opt-in prompt to ask what the 1940 map said about the ground under your feet, with a typed address fallback for visitors outside Chicago; the answer returns the grade, the surveyor's sheet, and one sourced sentence tying grade to present outcome. The page closes with the moderated answer wall, full credits and sources, and the files reading room as an annex below the fold.

artDirection: The site's existing cream, ink, forest, and rust palette stays, but with a strict pigment law. The archival HOLC green, blue, yellow, and red are reserved exclusively for grade data and never used decoratively, so red on this page always means the thing the map meant by it. The argument voice runs in the display serif in rust; evidence runs in ink on cream; surveyor and covenant language is set in a document face that reads as typescript without cosplaying as a typewriter font. The material logic is paper throughout. Every instrument enters as a document, presses like a stamp, prints its effect onto the ground, and the ink never lifts. Texture is restrained, flat archival-scan lighting, a one-pixel press shadow at most, no skeuomorphic grain. Motion has one verb, settle. Everything eases out and comes to rest like ink drying; nothing bounces, loops, or pulses. This fits the subject because the argument is that the harm was administrative, patient, and permanent, and the page should feel administrative, patient, and permanent.
interactionModel: Scroll is the only mandatory input, and it drives stepped sticky scenes, never pixel-scrubbed hijacked ones. Roughly once per chapter there is a single tap invitation with obvious affordance, such as opening the covenant deed, reading the surveyor sheet under the centered polygon, expanding a ledger entry, or touching a memorial roll entry to locate its point. There are exactly two deliberate acts of input, both near the end, granting location or typing an address, and writing on the answer wall. Every scene is step-indexed, so keyboard users move through the identical sequence of resolved states with arrow keys and skip links, and screen readers get a prose equivalent per step. The bombing act intentionally strips interaction down to plain reading plus one respectful tap.
mobileStrategy: On a 390px phone the ground plane lives as a sticky top panel of about 44vh with text cards scrolling beneath it, so the map is always visible while reading, and the instrument dock collapses to a five-glyph strip pinned above the ledger line, expanding on tap. All scrubbed scenes degrade to discrete steps fired by IntersectionObserver, each a fully resolved state, which is also the reduced-motion behavior, so the phone build and the accessibility build are the same build. The 703 polygons render as pre-baked canvas raster layers per map state with a lightweight SVG hit layer mounted only in chapters that invite tapping. Images ship as AVIF with reserved dimensions, the JS budget stays under roughly 250KB gzipped, and the Two Buyers and true-scale climb scenes are pure DOM and CSS transforms. A thin progress rail with the 13 chapter marks doubles as a jump map and a resume marker for the visitor who returns.
reuse: Keep the 703-polygon HOLC dataset and the 576 digitized surveyor sheets wholesale; they are the spine of the ground plane and the Grade Flood moment.

Rebuild the 2.5D relief turntable into the flat persistent ground plane. The turntable is a beautiful set piece, but it competes with the through-line by making the map a destination instead of the stage. Its relief rendering can survive as the cold-open hero frame only; the 7-stop turntable interaction goes.
Keep the no-motion bombing map and docket nearly as-is and re-typeset them into the memorial roll; that component already honors the dignity constraint.
Rebuild the two-lane Supreme Court current diagram as a stepped sticky scene with four gates; the metaphor is correct, the presentation becomes scroll-driven.
Rebuild the true-scale wealth-gap climb as the finale with era milestones along the tall column; keep its true-scale principle exactly, it becomes the page's closing signature.
Keep the files reading room with grade filters and permalinks, moved to the annex after the credits so the narrative flow never dumps the visitor into a database mid-story.
Keep the geolocation grade lookup and the moderated answer wall; both move to Act VII where they land as consequence rather than novelty.
Drop the framed evidence-station layout and the wall-text label blocks entirely; nothing of the document-flow presentation carries over.
risks: Performance of 703 animating polygons on mid-range phones. Mitigate with pre-baked canvas raster states plus an SVG hit layer mounted only when tapping is invited, and cap simultaneous layers at two.

Scrolljack temptation. Every scene must use position sticky plus stepped states; the moment the wheel is locked or remapped, keyboard and reduced-motion parity die and the museum feel dies with them. This is a hard implementation rule, not a preference.

Animated interpolation implying invented data. The covenant spread and clearance erasure may only move between dated, registry-sourced snapshot states, with the date and figure printed at each state; no tween may show a coverage value that does not resolve to a fact ID.

The bombing act's register break being read as a design flourish. Review that act against a single test, would a descendant of the two dead find every pixel respectful; if any element fails, cut it to plain text.

Page fatigue across 13 chapters. The progress rail, the short Act II palate cleanser, and hard caps on per-chapter card word counts (owner has rejected wall text once already) are the defense; if a chapter needs 400 words, the words are wrong.
The cold-open rewind confusing reduced-motion visitors. Provide the rewind as four labeled crossfade frames, 1940, 1908, 1853, 1832, so the sequence still reads as time moving backward.
Geolocation privacy and out-of-Chicago visitors. Lookup stays client-side and opt-in with a typed address or landmark fallback, and the copy never implies the site stored anything.
Dock crowding at 390px. The five-glyph collapsed strip must be tested with all five lit; if it reads as clutter, the strip shows only the currently active stamp with a tap to expand the set.

showDontTell.content: The 1940 HOLC map is an instrument of exclusion, not a historical illustration
showDontTell.treatment: The visitor meets the map cold, before any argument, then watches it get built piece by piece across five acts, and only in Act V does it recolor into the grades while the surveyors' own sentences sit beside each color. The page never says the map was a weapon. The visitor watches it become one.

showDontTell.content: Five instruments overlapped rather than succeeded each other
showDontTell.treatment: The persistent stamp dock lights one stamp per chapter and never dims any, and the overture's span chart lets the visitor sweep a now-line across 1908-1970 and see four bars lit at once. Overlap is a picture the thumb produces, not a sentence.

A memorial roll of 40 dated entries in plain type, the dead named large, and 0 convictions set alone as the final line of the act, with every page motion convention suspended. The silence of the layout carries the number.

showDontTell.content: Shelley and Hansberry voided the paper but not the practice
showDontTell.treatment: The Supreme Court gates open on screen while the covenant hatching already printed on the ground plane visibly stays. The visitor sees the law change and the ground not change.

showDontTell.content: Contract selling charged nearly double for the same house, $71,000 average overpayment
showDontTell.treatment: Two identical house elevations, twenty scrolled years, payment stubs stacking in real proportion under each. The contract pile physically outgrows the mortgage pile before any number is stated.

showDontTell.content: White median family wealth $285,010 versus Black $44,890 in 2022
showDontTell.treatment: A true-scale scroll. Passing the Black column takes one flick, passing the white column takes 6.35 times the distance with era milestones en route. The visitor's own scrolling effort is the chart.

showDontTell.content: The ground is still moving today
showDontTell.treatment: The ground plane, now carrying every mark from 1853 forward including the still-blank renewal parcels, zooms to the grade under the visitor's own feet. The past arrives at their location instead of being described to them.

signatureMoments.name: The Rewind
signatureMoments.description: Full-bleed 1940 HOLC map with only an archival caption. On scroll, a corner date counter runs 1940 back to 1832 while the map drains in four stepped states (grades out, grid thins, shoreline only, blank ground). Implemented as pre-baked raster crossfades under a sticky container, roughly 300vh of scroll. Reduced motion gets the same four frames as labeled crossfades. This is the shareable opening frame and it teaches the page's grammar in one gesture.

signatureMoments.name: The Stamp Dock
signatureMoments.description: Five engraved stamps with instrument names and year spans dock on the right rail (bottom strip on mobile). Each presses and lights at its chapter with a short settle transform and stays lit permanently. Tapping any stamp at any time opens a one-card definition with active years and the registry fact it rests on. State is a single integer per stamp, trivially keyboard focusable.

signatureMoments.name: The Grade Flood
signatureMoments.where: Act V, Washington adopts the plan
signatureMoments.description: The grades wash back onto the ground plane in archival pigment, area by area over four stepped states, while the digitized surveyor sheet for the polygon nearest screen center slides up with its verbatim description highlighted. Tap any polygon to swap the sheet. Canvas raster for fills, SVG hit layer for taps, sheet content from the existing 576-sheet dataset. The cold-open map is re-met as a document with an author.

signatureMoments.name: The Memorial Roll
signatureMoments.description: Single column, near-monochrome, 40 dated entries with addresses from the incident dataset, the two dead named in larger type, 0 convictions alone on the closing line. One static map plate with 32 points sits alongside. Tapping an entry strokes its point once. No sticky scenes, no counters, no parallax anywhere in the act. The register break is the moment; it must be felt as the page lowering its voice.

signatureMoments.name: The Two Buyers Stubs
signatureMoments.description: Sticky split scene, two identical line-drawn house elevations. Each scrolled year 1948-1968 drops a payment stub under both sides at true relative height from the financial model, mortgage side gaining equity shading, contract side showing the forfeiture clause on its stubs. Resolves on the $71,000 figure with source line. Pure DOM stubs, stepped per year, exactly 20 steps, identical for keyboard users.

signatureMoments.name: The True-Scale Climb
signatureMoments.description: Two columns rendered at true scale to scroll distance. $44,890 passes in about one viewport, $285,010 requires 6.35 viewports with milestone captions at proportional heights. A persistent small indicator shows how far up the white column the visitor has traveled. Ends level with a single sourced sentence. This is the screenshot moment and the argument's QED.

signatureMoments.name: The Grade Under Your Feet
signatureMoments.description: The ground plane returns bearing every accumulated mark. An opt-in prompt offers geolocation or a typed address. The answer zooms the plane, names the 1940 grade in its archival pigment, opens the surveyor sheet for that polygon, and prints one sourced sentence linking grade to present outcome. Client-side only, with a graceful out-of-area response offering a landmark picker.

thesis: The entire exhibit happens on one piece of ground that never leaves the screen. Five instruments enter as real documents, press like stamps, and print their marks onto that ground in sequence, and no mark is ever erased. By the time the 2026 wealth figures arrive, they read as the sum of everything the visitor watched accumulate, not as a claim they are asked to believe.
throughLine: Three persistent elements, layered. First, the Ground, a single sticky map plane of Hyde Park that is on screen from the cold open to the final scene and accumulates every mark (plat lines, purge outlines, covenant hatching, grade pigment, renewal blanks) without ever erasing one, so the 2026 map is visibly the 1853 map plus everything done to it. Second, the Instrument Dock, five document stamps that light as each instrument activates and never go dark, making overlap and persistence visible at all times. Third, the Ledger Strip along the bottom edge, which prints its 11 dated entries of dollars and people as the story reaches them and expands into the full account in the finale. Together they carry the timeline into the present because all three are still on screen, still marked, when the visitor's own location is looked up.
title: The Same Ground
visitorTakeaway: A week later the visitor remembers scrolling one map for two hundred years and watching it get taken, papered, graded, cleared, and priced twice, remembers their thumb taking six times longer to climb the white wealth column, and remembers that the red line they saw drawn in 1940 came back at the end under their own address. The sentence they repeat is that none of it was an accident, it was filed.

arc.chapters: Chapter 1 (The map)
arc.onScreen: Full-bleed flat 1940 HOLC map of Hyde Park and environs, ink linework on cream, initially UNGRADED, just the street grid and the lake. One caption line at the bottom edge, max 25 words. The visitor's first tap anywhere on the map inks the grades in, all 703 polygons at once, in the four true HOLC colors. A second caption appears with the source card for the map itself (fact id visible). Below the plate, a thin horizontal strip appears for the first time, five empty gray bars with a 1900 to 2026 axis. This is the Instrument Register and it never leaves the screen again. The map plate is now the fixed top pane of the page; everything for the next 12 chapters is a layer drawn onto or peeled off of this one plate.

arc.chapters: Chapters 2 and 3 (The first taking, The fair)
arc.onScreen: The grades fade to 10% and the plate rewinds. The 1853 plat lines overlay the same geography (the visitor sees that the modern grid IS the plat, same viewport, same scale, layering not slideshow). The Potawatomi cession is drawn as the boundary it was, with the 1833 treaty entry opening the Ledger Rail, a narrow right-margin running account (dollars and people, tabular figures, 11 entries total by page end). The 1893 fair appears as a footprint layer plus one credited archival photograph in a caption drawer. Total visitor text in this act is under 120 words.

arc.chapters: Chapter 4 (Five instruments)
arc.onScreen: The map dims to a ghost and the Instrument Register expands to fill the pane. Five horizontal bars on one shared time axis, realtors' rule 1921-1950, covenants 1927-1948, HOLC/FHA 1934-1968, urban renewal 1952 onward, contract selling 1952-1970. The bars overlap. A single annotation line reads the thesis off the graphic itself. From 1921 to 1970 at least one instrument is always running; when a court kills one, the next is already in place. Handoff points (Shelley 1948, for example) get small tick annotations. This graphic then shrinks back to its permanent strip position, where a date cursor will ride it for the rest of the page showing which instruments are live in the current chapter. The relay IS the argument, seen before it is read.

arc.chapters: Chapters 5 and 6 (The purge, The bombing years)
arc.onScreen: The purge chapter draws the homeowners club's target blocks on the plate with the club's own printed language available on tap. Then the bombing chapter. The plate goes nearly monochrome. 32 fixed black dots appear at their addresses, no motion, no sequencing animation. Below the plate, the Docket, a formally typeset table, one row per dated incident (40 rows), columns for date, address, outcome. The outcome column is typographically present and blank in every row. A closing totals row in tabular figures reads bombings 58, killed 2, convictions 0. Ida B. Wells's quote is pinned in the margin at its date. The emptiness of the column is the entire graphic. Nothing here moves, ever.

arc.chapters: Chapter 7 (The paperwork)
arc.onScreen: Article 34 of the realtors' code appears alone on cream at display size, one sentence, its own source card. The Register strip lights the first bar. Then the covenant layer. Parcels on the plate fill with a fine diagonal signature hatch (a pattern sampled from an actual scanned covenant page) as the visitor drags a year slider from 1927 to 1948. If recorded dates per tract are not in the fact registry, the slider degrades honestly to two states, before and at peak. Tapping any hatched parcel opens the actual deed clause scan with the restrictive language highlighted. A covenant is thus SHOWN as what it was, a paragraph of paperwork multiplied across land.

arc.chapters: Chapter 8 (Washington adopts the plan)
arc.onScreen: The grades ink back in at full strength, and this time every one of the 703 polygons is tappable. Tap a polygon, get its actual surveyor area-description sheet, the scan on one side, the transcribed remarks line pulled out beside it. The 576-sheet reading room lives entirely behind this gesture (detail on demand, not a separate station). One D-grade sheet and one A-grade sheet are pre-opened as a side-by-side pair so the visitor sees the language difference before choosing their own. The Ledger Rail posts the federal dollar entries. The caption states plainly that the private map became federal underwriting policy, under 40 words.

arc.chapters: Chapter 9 (The walls crack)
arc.onScreen: A 2x2 small multiple of the four Supreme Court cases, Buchanan 1917, Corrigan 1926, Hansberry 1940, Shelley 1948, each rendered in the identical two-lane diagram (claim lane, ruling lane) so the eye compares outcomes structurally. Hansberry's own words are pinned to the Washington Park subdivision on the plate. The Register strip shows the covenant bar terminating at 1948 while the FHA bar runs on and two new bars are about to start. The annotation points at that continuity, not at the victory.

arc.act: Act 7. The Bulldozer and the Contract
arc.chapters: Chapters 10 and 11 (The university rebuilds, The color tax)
arc.onScreen: Renewal first. 638 building footprints on the plate turn from solid to outline (cleared to void), stepped by project phase with a scrub control, honoring reduced motion. Beneath it, the family grid, one small square per family, about 4,000 marks in a canvas grid roughly 80 wide by 50 tall, labeled 'about 4,000 families, each mark is one, the count is the source's estimate.' The visitor must scroll past all of them. Then the color tax. Two Buyers, one house, side by side, month-by-month payment columns on a shared money axis over the full term. The contract buyer's line runs above the mortgage buyer's; the area between them is shaded and its integral labeled at true scale, $71,000, with the era's median income drawn on the same axis for reference. Dempsey Travis and Clyde Ross are pinned in the margin. A slider scrubs the months.

arc.chapters: Chapter 12 (The Contract Buyers League)
arc.onScreen: The identical Two Buyers chart returns, an encoding the visitor has already learned, now annotated with the CBL payment strike and renegotiations, the gap visibly narrowing where the registry supports it. The win is legible as a change in a chart, not as prose. Ruth Wells speaks from a church basement photograph in the caption drawer. This is the only act whose ledger entry runs in the visitor's favor, and the Ledger Rail marks it.

arc.act: Act 9. The Ledger and the Ground
arc.chapters: Chapter 13 (The ledger and the ground today)
arc.onScreen: First, the full plate with every layer toggled on at once, plat, dots, hatch, grades, voids, one dense supergraphic with a layer legend the visitor can flip themselves. Then the plate slides up and off, revealing the wealth climb at true pixel scale, $285,010 white median beside $44,890 Black median, same scale, no truncation; on a phone the visitor scrolls the full height of the white bar to reach its label, and the scroll distance is the encoding. Then the geolocation moment. 'The grade under your feet,' a one-tap lookup printed as a plain receipt card, polygon id, 1940 grade, the surveyor's remark verbatim, source line. Baldwin and King close the margin quotes. The moderated answer wall sits last, after the argument, never interrupting it.

artDirection: Archival print, not app chrome. Base is the site cream, linework in ink, hairline rules, flat light, zero drop shadows and zero gradients, so the page reads like a museum table case holding a period document. The four HOLC colors (green, blue, yellow, red) are reserved EXCLUSIVELY for grades A through D and appear nowhere else on the page, not in buttons, not in accents, so color is always an honest encoding. Rust (the site accent) is reserved for exactly one meaning, present-day consequence, so when rust appears in the Ledger Rail and the wealth climb the visitor has been trained to read it as 'this is now.' Typography per house style, display serif for the few large statements (Article 34, chapter titles), body face elsewhere, tabular lining figures mandatory in the Docket, the Ledger Rail, and every axis. The Docket is set like a court record, small caps column heads, generous leading, because dignity here is typographic. Data-ink discipline throughout, no icons where a number can stand, no illustration where a scanned document exists. The 15 archival photographs are the only halftone texture on the page and therefore carry enormous weight; they get full-column width, a credit line, and nothing overlaid on them.
interactionModel: Two gestures, learned once in chapter 1 and never changed. ADVANCE (tap the next control or step-scroll) moves between the 13 chapters; the map plate persists and only its layers change, so advancing feels like turning acetate overlays on a light table, not loading pages. INSPECT (tap any mark, polygon, dot, hatched parcel, unit square region, or any on-screen number) opens a source card from the 126-fact registry with the figure, the citation, and where applicable the scanned primary document. Detail on demand is literally the fact registry made touchable; the 576 surveyor sheets, the deed clauses, and the docket rows are all behind this one gesture. Two scrub sliders exist (covenant years, Two Buyers months) and one layer-legend toggle set in the finale; nothing on the page ever autoplays. Expected rhythm is one deliberate touch every 20 to 40 seconds for roughly 8 to 12 minutes, with the reading room and files available for visitors who want an hour.
mobileStrategy: The plate architecture is designed phone-first. On 390px the map plate is a fixed top pane of 45vh with pinch-zoom and an inset locator; the caption drawer and evidence graphics occupy the bottom 55vh and advance with a persistent prev/next bar (also full keyboard path and step-scroll). The Instrument Register collapses to a five-tick strip 24px tall that expands full-screen on tap. The 703 polygons ship as one simplified-geometry JSON rendered to a single SVG (one path per grade for fills, per-polygon hit layer), well under 300KB; the 4,000-mark family grid renders in canvas, not DOM. The Docket becomes stacked rows that preserve the blank outcome cell per row and the totals row. The wealth climb keeps true scale by using scroll length as the axis, which is native and free on a phone. Surveyor sheet scans and archival photographs lazy-load at tap time only. Reduced-motion visitors lose nothing because nothing essential moves; sliders step discretely instead of tweening. Screen readers get the Docket and Ledger Rail as real HTML tables, every polygon as a named button, and a prose equivalent of each act's graphic in an aria-described summary.
reuse: KEEP the 703-polygon geometry, grade join, and surveyor-sheet linkage from the existing SVG map, but RE-PLATFORM it from the 2.5D relief turntable to a flat orthographic plate. The third dimension and the seven-stop rotation encode nothing; relief here is chartjunk and it costs mobile performance. Flat plate, honest projection, persistent position.

KEEP the no-motion bombing map and docket nearly intact; it already meets the dignity constraint. Rework only the typography (court-record setting, blank outcome column made structurally visible, totals row) and dock it beneath the persistent plate instead of standing alone.
KEEP the true-scale wealth climb concept and its pixel-honest ratio; rebind it to scroll length on mobile and move it to the finale position after the all-layers supergraphic.

KEEP the files reading room (grade filters, permalinks, 576 searchable sheets) as the destination behind polygon taps, demoted from a standalone station to the detail-on-demand layer; its permalink URLs stay for citation.

REBUILD the two-lane Supreme Court current diagram as a 2x2 small multiple with identical axes so the four cases compare structurally at a glance; the existing single-case version buries the comparison.
KEEP the geolocation grade lookup and reframe its output as a printed receipt card with polygon id, grade, verbatim remark, and source line.

DROP the document-flow label blocks and framed evidence stations entirely. The wall of prose is the enemy; every retired paragraph either becomes a caption under 40 words, a pinned marginal quote, or a source card behind a tap.

BUILD NEW: the Instrument Register (persistent five-bar relay strip), the Ledger Rail (11-entry running account), the covenant hatch layer with deed-clause taps, the Two Buyers paired payment chart with shaded gap, and the 4,000-mark family grid.
risks: The relay thesis lives or dies on the Instrument Register being readable at 24px collapsed height on a phone; if the five bars are illegible there, the through-line breaks. Mitigate with a one-tap full-screen expansion and a current-date cursor that is legible even in the strip.

Covenant recording dates per tract may not exist in the fact registry at year granularity; the year slider must be built to degrade to two honest states (pre-1927, peak coverage) rather than interpolating an invented spread. Real data only means the interaction design cannot assume data density.

703 polygons plus pattern hatches plus a persistent fixed pane is a real mid-range-phone rendering budget; if the plate janks, the whole light-table metaphor collapses. Budget it early, one merged path per grade, canvas for unit grids, no re-mounting the SVG between chapters, and test on an actual mid-range device before polish.

A persistent fixed pane plus step-advance flirts with scroll-jacking; if native scroll is fought rather than used, mobile visitors will bounce. Use CSS scroll-snap on discrete act sections with the plate position:sticky, never JS-hijacked wheel events.
The 'about 4,000 families' unit grid must carry its approximation notice visibly or it becomes a false-precision graphic; the label is part of the encoding, not a footnote.

The finale supergraphic (all layers on) risks illegibility, which would read as chaos rather than accumulation; it needs a designed default layer order and opacity plan, verified in both themes, with the legend toggles as the escape hatch.

Two scrub sliders and hundreds of tappable marks create a large keyboard-path surface; the accessibility pass must be scheduled as build work, not audit work, especially the polygon hit layer as named buttons.

showDontTell.content: Exclusion was engineered, not accidental (the central argument)
showDontTell.treatment: The Instrument Register. Five bars on one shared time axis, permanently on screen, showing that from 1921 to 1970 at least one instrument is always running and every court defeat is followed by a handoff already in progress. Continuity of coverage is visible as overlapping ink before a single sentence claims it. The date cursor riding the strip through all 13 chapters makes the visitor watch the relay happen.

The Docket. Forty typeset rows with a structurally present, entirely blank outcome column, closed by a totals row in tabular figures. The zero is not stated in prose; it is the white space the visitor scrolls past forty times. Thirty-two fixed dots on the monochrome plate, no motion of any kind.

Not a definition. A fine signature hatch spreading across real parcels on the plate as the visitor drags the year slider, and behind any tap, the actual scanned deed paragraph with the restrictive clause highlighted. A covenant is shown as one paragraph of paperwork multiplied across land.

Two Buyers, one house. Paired month-by-month payment columns on a shared money axis; the shaded area between the two series IS the $71,000, labeled at true scale with the era's median income on the same axis for size reference. The visitor scrubs the months and watches the gap accumulate payment by payment.

showDontTell.content: About 4,000 families displaced by university-era renewal
showDontTell.treatment: One mark, one family. A canvas grid of roughly 4,000 small squares the visitor must physically scroll past, labeled as an estimate, paired with 638 building footprints turning from solid to void on the plate. The magnitude is experienced as scroll distance and mark count before the number is read.

showDontTell.content: The 2022 wealth gap, white $285,010 vs Black $44,890
showDontTell.treatment: True scale or nothing. Both bars on one pixel scale with no axis break; on a phone the visitor scrolls the full height of the white bar to reach its label. The 6-to-1 ratio is felt in the thumb.
Article 34 set alone at display size on an otherwise empty cream screen, one sentence, one source card. The smallness of the instrument against the size of its consequence is the graphic.

showDontTell.content: The private map became federal policy (1933-1940)
showDontTell.treatment: The same 703 polygons the visitor already knows become tappable doors to their actual surveyor sheets, with a pre-opened A-grade and D-grade pair side by side so the difference in official language is read off primary paper, not paraphrase.

The identical Two Buyers chart returns with the strike and renegotiations annotated and the shaded gap visibly narrowing. Because the visitor already learned this encoding two chapters earlier, the victory is legible as a change in a picture they know.

The grade under your feet. A geolocation tap returns a plain receipt card with the visitor's 1940 polygon, grade, and the surveyor's verbatim remark. The 86-year-old paperwork addresses the visitor personally, in the present tense of their own location.

signatureMoments.name: The Relay (Instrument Register)
signatureMoments.where: Introduced full-screen in Act 2, then persistent as a strip beneath the plate through every subsequent chapter
signatureMoments.description: Five horizontal bars on one 1900-2026 axis, one per instrument, with true start and end dates. Full-screen version carries handoff annotations at the joints (for example, covenant enforcement ends 1948 while the FHA bar runs on and contract selling begins 1952). Collapsed version is a 24px strip with a moving date cursor showing which bars are live at the current chapter's date; tapping expands it. Built as one small SVG, dates bound to registry fact ids, cursor position derived from the active act. This is the page's thesis rendered as a single honest Gantt, and it must be the most carefully typeset object on the page.

signatureMoments.name: The Empty Column (Docket)
signatureMoments.where: Act 3, beneath the monochrome plate with its 32 static dots
signatureMoments.description: An HTML table, real semantics, one row per dated incident (40 rows), columns Date, Address, Outcome, set in court-record style with small caps heads and tabular figures. Outcome cells are rendered, bordered, and empty for every row. Final totals row, bombings 58, killed 2, convictions 0, each figure tapping through to its source card. No animation, no hover effects, no color. Screen readers announce each empty cell as 'no conviction recorded' via an accessible label agreed with the registry wording.

signatureMoments.name: Two Buyers, One House
signatureMoments.where: Act 7 (color tax) and reprised with strike annotations in Act 8 (CBL)
signatureMoments.description: A paired column chart, months on the x axis across the full purchase term, dollars on a shared y axis, mortgage buyer and contract buyer as two series from the same registry-backed financial model. The area between the series is shaded and labeled with its integral, $71,000, at true scale, with period median household income drawn as a reference line on the same axis. A discrete month scrub (slider plus keyboard arrows) reveals the accumulation; reduced motion gets the final state by default. The Act 8 reprise overlays the payment strike period and the renegotiated terms where the registry supports them, and nowhere else.

signatureMoments.name: One Mark, One Family
signatureMoments.where: Act 7, immediately after the 638 footprints void out on the plate
signatureMoments.description: A canvas-rendered unit grid, approximately 4,000 squares at 3 to 4px with 2px gutters, about 80 per row on desktop and reflowing on mobile, in a single ink tone. Header label reads 'about 4,000 families, each mark is one; the count is the source's estimate' with the estimate's fact id tappable. The grid is tall enough that the visitor scrolls through it; no interaction per mark is claimed (the marks are anonymous and the design says so), one tap anywhere opens the source card for the displacement estimate.

signatureMoments.name: The Climb at True Scale
signatureMoments.where: Act 9, after the all-layers supergraphic, before the geolocation receipt
signatureMoments.description: Two vertical bars, white median family wealth $285,010 and Black median family wealth $44,890 (2022), drawn on one shared pixel scale with zero baseline and no break. On mobile the bars exceed the viewport by design and the page scrolls along them; gridlines every $25,000 tick past as the visitor climbs, in rust because this is the present day. Labels sit at each bar's true top. Both figures tap to source cards. No percentage framing, no ratio callout until the visitor has traversed the height; the ratio sentence appears only at the summit.

signatureMoments.name: The Grade Under Your Feet
signatureMoments.where: Final beat of Act 9, above the answer wall
signatureMoments.description: A single button requesting geolocation (with a typed-address fallback for denial or out-of-area). The result is a receipt-styled card, monospace-adjacent tabular setting: polygon id, 1940 grade with its true HOLC color swatch, the surveyor's remark quoted verbatim from the joined sheet, and the source line. If the visitor is outside graded Chicago, the card says so plainly and offers the Hyde Park polygon the page has been standing on instead. The card has a copy-link permalink into the reading room.

thesis: One map, held on screen for the entire visit, accumulates the evidence layer by layer the way the exclusion itself accumulated, plat, dots, hatch, grades, voids, until the visitor has personally assembled the machine. A persistent five-bar Instrument Register beneath it shows the relay at true scale, no gap in coverage from 1921 to 1970, so the claim 'engineered, not accidental' is seen as continuous ink before it is ever read as a sentence. Every number is an encoding first (a blank column, a shaded gap, a scroll-length bar, one mark per family) and a tappable source card second, with prose demoted to captions under 40 words.
throughLine: Two persistent objects carry the whole page. First, the Plate, the flat 1940 map that never leaves the screen; every chapter draws a layer onto it or peels one off (1853 plat, bombing dots, covenant hatch, HOLC grades, renewal voids), so by the finale the visitor watches all layers stack into one supergraphic they built themselves, and then the plate physically yields to the present-day wealth climb and the grade-under-your-feet receipt. Second, the Instrument Register, the five-bar relay strip introduced in the overture and docked beneath the plate ever after, its date cursor riding forward chapter by chapter until the bars end and only the 2026 ledger remains. The Ledger Rail (11 entries, 1833 to 2026, rust for the present) runs in the margin as the quiet third thread connecting every dollar to the final wealth figures.
title: The Plate and the Register
visitorTakeaway: A week later the visitor remembers three pictures, not paragraphs. Five overlapping bars with no gap for fifty years, which is what 'engineered' looks like. A court docket with forty entries and an outcome column that is entirely blank. And the length of their own thumb-scroll up a $285,010 bar after standing, via their phone's location, on a block that federal paperwork graded in 1940. The argument survives as retinal memory, exclusion ran continuously, on paper, with public money, and the receipt is dated 2022.

arc.chapters: Chapter 1 (The map)
arc.onScreen: The page opens as a darkened room. No site header, no title, no navigation. The 1940 HOLC map of Chicago's South Side fills the viewport under a soft spotlight vignette, rendered flat and still, its 703 areas in their true grade colors against near-black. One line of wall text sits beneath it, small serif, museum-label size. The visitor taps or keys to any area and a flat-file drawer slides up from the bottom edge carrying the actual scanned surveyor sheet for that polygon, the grade chip, and a button reading 'show what the surveyor wrote' that raises the typed sentence in highlight. Close the drawer, the room is silent again. Only after the visitor scrolls past the map does the exhibit title appear, alone on a dark wall, with one sentence stating the argument. A thin black surveyor's ink line begins at the title and runs down the left margin. It will not stop until 2026.

arc.chapters: Chapters 2 and 3 (The first taking, The fair)
arc.onScreen: The walls lighten slightly, the first and brightest room. A single vitrine holds the 1853 plat, presented large on a cream mat with a hairline rule, the Potawatomi treaty stated in two label sentences with its registry mark. Then one full-bleed plate, the 1893 fair photograph, captioned with what the fair built and who it was built without. Two artifacts, four sentences of wall text, nothing else. The ink line runs quietly through the room. This act exists so the visitor knows the ground had a history before the paperwork arrived, and so the compression ahead has something to compress from.

arc.chapters: Chapter 4 (Five instruments overture)
arc.onScreen: Five plinths in a row, stacked vertically on a phone. Each plinth carries a facsimile fragment of an actual document under glass. Article 34 of the realtors' code. A deed page with its covenant clause. A HOLC area description sheet. An urban renewal ordinance page. A land installment contract. Above each, a brass roman numeral, I through V, with the instrument's name and working dates. The wall text is three plain sentences making the argument explicit, that exclusion was engineered, that these five documents did it, that it ran on paperwork and public money. Each numeral becomes gallery signage. From here on, every room downstream carries the small brass numeral of whichever instrument is operating in it, so the visitor always knows which part of the machine they are watching.

arc.act: Act 4. Removal by Committee, Removal by Dynamite
arc.chapters: Chapters 5 and 6 (The purge, The bombing years)
arc.onScreen: The corridor compresses. Margins narrow, the wall value drops to the darkest in the exhibit. The purge is told through typeset minutes of the homeowners club, an excerpt in period type inside a plain frame, with a two-sentence label. Then the Docket Wall. Forty dated entries set in a court-record face, one per row, address, date, damage, all sourced. No motion of any kind, no counters, no map animation. The two people killed are named mid-wall in larger type at eye level, with their names given more space than anything else in the room. The final line stands alone with air above and below it, zero convictions. A single static map plate with the 32 placeable incidents sits after the docket as evidence, captioned, not interactive. The visitor exits through a bench, one Ida B. Wells quotation alone on the dark wall, then empty space before the next room. This is the one room where interaction is deliberately withdrawn. The visitor's only act here is to walk past every name at their own pace.

arc.chapters: Chapters 7 and 8 (The paperwork, Washington adopts the plan)
arc.onScreen: Numerals I, II, and III hang at the room entrance. The visitor pulls a document sleeve and a facsimile deed opens; a button reading 'read the clause' raises the racial restriction in the deed's own typeface, with the signature and recording stamp visible, because a covenant was signed by a neighbor and filed by a clerk. Then three HOLC drawers, each yielding a real scanned area sheet with the D-grade language highlighted on request. Washington's adoption is shown, not narrated, by two letterheads side by side in one vitrine, the Chicago realtors' rule and the federal underwriting language that repeats it, with the years between them stated in the label. At the moment the federal page appears, the ink line running down the margin turns HOLC D-grade red. It stays red for the rest of the exhibit.

arc.chapters: Chapter 9 (Hansberry, Shelley)
arc.onScreen: A release room, the wall value rises. Four case folders in a row, Buchanan 1917, Corrigan 1926, Hansberry 1940, Shelley 1948. Opening a folder gives the holding in two sentences and, crucially, a line stating what the ruling did not stop, drawn from the rebuilt two-lane current diagram, restaged here as two labeled channels showing which instruments each decision closed and which kept flowing. Hansberry's folder carries the address on South Rhodes and Lorraine Hansberry's verbatim words as the voice of the room. The label makes the curatorial point without swagger, that the courts cracked the covenant and the money simply changed instruments.

arc.chapters: Chapter 10 (The university rebuilds the neighborhood)
arc.onScreen: Numeral IV. A figure-ground plate of Hyde Park block footprints fills the frame, every demolished building hairline-outlined. The visitor drags a pull-tab slider between the pre-clearance plate and the post-clearance plate, at their own hand speed, no autoplay. The label states 638 buildings and about 4,000 families with their registry marks, and nothing more, because the plates carry the room. One large archival clearance photograph follows, captioned with street and year. A short bench after, one Dempsey Travis or James Baldwin quotation alone on the wall.

arc.act: Act 8. The Color Tax and the Basement
arc.chapters: Chapters 11 and 12 (Contract selling, Contract Buyers League)
arc.onScreen: Numeral V. Two receipts hang side by side for the same house, one headed Mortgage Buyer, one headed Contract Buyer. As the visitor scrolls, the line items pay out in step on both receipts, down payment, monthly payment, equity held, eviction exposure, every figure from the Two Buyers model. The totals close $71,000 apart. The difference detaches as a small paper stub that the visitor will meet again in the final room. Then the light warms, the single warmest room in the exhibit. The church basement photograph, large. Ruth Wells and Clyde Ross in their own verbatim words. The payment strike and the win stated in three plain sentences. Martin Luther King Jr.'s words close the room. The exhibit's only victory is staged as its most human room.

arc.act: Act 9. The Ledger and the Ground
arc.chapters: Chapter 13 (The ledger and the ground today)
arc.onScreen: The final room, and the longest wall. First the 11-entry ledger, 1833 to 2026, set as a single tall account column in the court-record face, each entry dated, dollared, and peopled, the $71,000 stub from Act 8 slotting into its row. Then the True-Scale Climb. The Black median family wealth bar, $44,890, fits inside one viewport. The white median bar, $285,010, requires roughly six more viewports of the visitor's own scrolling to pass, with quiet margin markers noting when the Black median was passed. The scroll itself is the exhibit. Then the personal station, opt-in only. The visitor grants location and receives a small printed archival card, styled as a catalog card, giving the 1940 grade under their feet, the area number, the grade color as the card's edge, and one sourced line from that area's surveyor sheet. The exit holds the visitor book, the moderated answer wall with a single question above it, then the colophon crediting every one of the 126 registry facts, and a plain door labeled Study Room leading to the files reading room annex for those who want the full 576 sheets.

artDirection: The exhibit abandons the site's cream daylight at a marked threshold and becomes a dark gallery, walls in a near-black warm ink, because the subject is an archive and archives are best read under a lamp. Artifacts sit on cream paper cards with hairline mats, the only surfaces carrying texture, so paper reads as paper against matte walls. Color is rationed with evidentiary discipline. The four HOLC grade colors appear only when they mean a grade, never as decoration, and the sole saturated accent in the entire exhibit is D-grade red, spent almost entirely on the spine line. Typography is two voices, a text serif for wall labels at true museum-didactic scale (short, wide-margined, never more than about sixty words per label) and a typewriter monospace for everything the machine produced, deeds, dockets, receipts, ledgers, catalog cards. Brass hairline rules and roman numerals do the signage. Light is the pacing instrument, exactly as in a physical gallery. Each room shifts the background value a step, brightest for 1832 and 1893, darkest for the bombing years, warm for the church basement, and the visitor feels the rooms change without being told. Photography runs full-bleed as plates with one-line credits. All contrast ratios hold WCAG AA on the dark walls. This direction fits the subject because the machinery was clerical and quiet, and a quiet, dark, precise room makes a typed sentence feel like what it was, a weapon.
interactionModel: One gesture family governs the whole exhibit. The visitor pulls things out of the archive. Drawers yield surveyor sheets, sleeves yield deeds, folders yield case files, a pull-tab compares clearance plates, a scroll pays out two receipts, an opt-in tap prints one catalog card. Every station is a labeled button or draggable handle, fully keyboard operable, reversible, and nothing anywhere autoplays. Density is one hands-on station per room, never two demands in the same viewport, so scrolling is the walk and touching is the choice. The bombing room deliberately offers no station at all; withdrawal of interaction is itself the design there. Between stations the visitor simply reads short labels and passes plates, which keeps hands busy roughly once per minute without turning history into a toy.
mobileStrategy: The 390px phone is the design master, not an adaptation. The flat-file drawer is natively a bottom sheet on a phone, so the exhibit's core gesture is a standard mobile pattern. Plinths, folders, and receipts stack single-column, and the docket wall is already a single column by nature. The red spine line becomes a 3px rule at the left screen edge doubling as scroll progress, which means the through-line costs no width. The True-Scale Climb is strongest on a phone because the scroll distance is longer and more physical. Engineering budget is strict for mid-range hardware, transform and opacity animation only, IntersectionObserver for room transitions, the map SVG code-split and loaded at the threshold, all 576 sheet scans lazy-loaded per tap with low-quality placeholders, pinned scroll scenes capped at two (map room and receipts) each with a static reduced-motion fallback, and no canvas or WebGL anywhere. Tap targets 44px minimum, and every drawer, folder, and slider is a real button or input reachable by keyboard and named for screen readers.
reuse: SVG 2.5D relief map (703 areas). Keep the geometry, grade data, and hit areas, which are the expensive part, but rebuild the presentation as the still, dark Map Room and drop the 7-stop turntable entirely. A turntable is spectacle; a map under a lamp is evidence.

Files reading room with grade filters and permalinks. Keep intact but relocate. It leaves the main visitor path and becomes the Study Room annex behind a labeled door at the exit, exactly as a museum keeps its study collection off the gallery floor. Its permalinks are reused by the drawer component.
True-scale wealth-gap climb. Keep the concept unchanged, since it is already the correct museum move, and restyle it to the gallery palette with margin markers and registry marks.

No-motion bombing map with docket. Keep the docket data and its restraint, but promote the docket to the wall itself with the memorial typography described above, and demote the map to one static captioned plate. The docket, not the map, is the artifact.
Two-lane Supreme Court current diagram. Keep, lightly reworked, folded inside the four case folders in Act 6 so it answers the specific question each ruling raises, what kept flowing.
Client-side geolocation grade lookup. Keep the lookup, restage the output as the printed catalog card in the final room, opt-in, on-device, never stored.
Moderated visitor answer wall. Keep, restaged as the visitor book at the exit with one question posted above it.
The current page's label-block and evidence-station layout system. Drop. It is the thing the owner scrolls past, and none of its framing carries into the gallery.
risks: The dark gallery palette breaks with the site's cream identity. Mitigated by a marked entry threshold (the visitor visibly walks into a room) and by returning to site chrome at the exit, but the owner must approve the divergence explicitly before build.

Two pinned scroll scenes plus a 703-polygon SVG can stutter on mid-range phones. Mitigated by code-splitting the map, transform-only animation, and static reduced-motion fallbacks, but the map room needs a performance budget test on a real $200 Android before anything else is built.

Nine rooms is a long walk and fatigue is the failure mode the owner already named. Mitigated by two benches, room-value light changes that make progress feel spatial, and a persistent gallery map (a small tap-to-open floor plan listing the nine rooms with jump links), but Acts 2 and 6 must stay ruthlessly short or the middle sags.

The drawer metaphor turns cute if overused. Discipline is one gesture family, one station per room, and zero novelty interactions outside it; any reviewer who finds a second gesture family should strike it.
576 lazy-loaded scans and 15 archival plates are a bandwidth cliff. Every image needs sized variants and low-quality placeholders, and the drawer must render its label text before its scan arrives.
Geolocation is a privacy risk and a trust risk on this subject. Opt-in only, computed on-device, never transmitted or stored, and the card must say so in its own footer line.

The bombing room will be judged by descendants. Its docket typography, naming hierarchy, and total absence of interaction must be reviewed by the owner as a standalone sign-off before launch, separate from the rest of the page.

showDontTell.treatment: Not a chart and not a counter. A typeset docket wall the visitor walks past at their own pace, forty sourced rows in a court-record face, the two names given the most space in the room, and the line zero convictions set alone with air around it. The visitor's own slow scroll past every row is the experience of the count.

A facsimile deed the visitor opens by hand, with the racial clause raised in the deed's own typeface beside a visible signature line and recording stamp. The visitor sees that a neighbor signed it and a clerk filed it, which is the entire argument about paperwork made physical.

Two letterheads in one vitrine, the Chicago realtors' rule and the federal underwriting language that repeats it, with the gap in years stated in a two-sentence label. The rhyme between the two documents is shown, and at that exact scroll position the margin spine turns from surveyor's ink to D-grade red.

A visitor-controlled pull-tab slider between two figure-ground plates, before and after clearance, every demolished footprint hairline-outlined. The visitor erases the blocks with their own hand, at their own speed, and the numbers appear only as a small sourced label.

showDontTell.content: Contract selling and the $71,000 average overpayment (1948-1970)
showDontTell.treatment: Two receipts for the same house paying out line by line under the visitor's scroll, mortgage buyer and contract buyer, until the totals close $71,000 apart and the difference tears off as a stub that reappears as a row in the final ledger.

True scale, no chart compression. The Black median bar fits one phone screen; passing the white median bar costs the visitor about six more screens of their own scrolling, with a quiet margin marker where the Black median was left behind. The visitor's thumb does the arithmetic.

showDontTell.content: The five instruments as a deliberate machine
showDontTell.treatment: Five real document fragments on five plinths with brass numerals, seen together before any of them is explained, then each numeral recurring as room signage downstream. The visitor learns the machine as a museum key and then watches each part operate in sequence.

showDontTell.content: The 1940 HOLC grades and their surveyor reasoning
showDontTell.treatment: The map alone in a dark room as the exhibit's single opening object, and the scanned sheets pulled from drawers area by area, with the typed sentence about race highlighted only when the visitor asks to see it. The grade colors appear nowhere else in the exhibit, so they never dilute into decoration.

An opt-in catalog card printing the 1940 grade under the visitor's own feet, edge-colored in that grade, quoting one sourced line from that area's sheet. Eighty-six-year-old paperwork addresses the visitor personally, in the present tense of their location.

signatureMoments.name: The Drawer of Sheets
signatureMoments.where: Act 1, the Map Room (and reused wherever a HOLC sheet appears)
signatureMoments.description: Tapping or keying to any of the 703 map areas slides a flat-file drawer up from the bottom edge (a bottom sheet on phones, a side drawer on desktop). The drawer contains the area number, the grade chip in true grade color, the lazily loaded scan of the actual surveyor sheet, and one button labeled 'show what the surveyor wrote' that raises the racially explicit typed line in a highlight the visitor chose to see. Each drawer state is permalinkable, reusing the existing reading-room permalink scheme. Drawer text renders before the scan arrives so the interaction never feels broken on slow networks.

signatureMoments.name: The Five Plinths
signatureMoments.description: Five document fragments under glass, each on a cream card with a hairline mat, each headed by a brass roman numeral, instrument name, and working dates. Built as one component with five data entries from the fact registry. Each numeral is minted once here and then reused as a small fixed badge at the entrance of every downstream room where that instrument operates, giving the whole page a signage system a developer can implement as a single RoomMark component.

signatureMoments.name: The Docket Wall
signatureMoments.description: Forty rows in a monospace court-record face, each row carrying date, address, damage, and source mark, generated from the 40-incident dataset. Row height, rhythm, and rule weights are fixed; no entrance animation, no counters, no hover states beyond focus outlines. The two victims' names are set in the serif at roughly three times body size mid-wall. The final standalone line reads zero convictions with a full viewport-height of dark wall above and below it. Screen readers receive the wall as a properly headed table with a caption.

signatureMoments.name: The Two Receipts
signatureMoments.description: Two receipt columns headed Mortgage Buyer and Contract Buyer for the same house, line items from the Two Buyers model paying out in step as the visitor scrolls (scroll-linked, transform-only, with a static full-length fallback under reduced motion). Totals land $71,000 apart. The difference then renders as a small perforated stub element that reappears, same component, as the matching row in the Act 9 ledger, giving the developer a literal shared component carrying the number forward.

signatureMoments.name: The Six-Screen Climb
signatureMoments.description: A true-scale vertical comparison where one pixel-per-dollar ratio is fixed for both bars. The $44,890 bar completes within the first viewport. The $285,010 bar continues for roughly six more viewports of ordinary scrolling, with small margin markers at the moment the Black median is passed and at each $50,000 rule. No easing, no parallax, nothing to make the distance shorter or prettier. The distance is the exhibit.

signatureMoments.name: The Card for Your Ground
signatureMoments.description: An opt-in button labeled plainly asks for location, computes the containing 1940 polygon on-device with the existing lookup, and renders a catalog card, area number, grade letter, grade color on the card edge, one sourced line from that area's sheet, and a footer line stating the location never left the device. Visitors outside graded Chicago receive a card explaining that their ground was never graded and what that fact itself means, so the moment fails gracefully everywhere on earth.

thesis: Stage the page as one dark gallery corridor built around a single opening artifact, the 1940 map, and five instruments displayed as real paperwork the visitor pulls from drawers, sleeves, and folders with their own hands. Scroll is the walk through nine rooms whose light levels, compression, and benches are paced like a physical museum, and a single red line drawn down the margin is the handrail that starts as surveyor's ink in 1832, turns HOLC red when Washington adopts the plan, and ends under the visitor's own feet in 2026. The argument is made by artifact hierarchy rather than prose, because the machinery was clerical, and clerical evidence shown at nameplate scale in a quiet room is more damning than any chart.
throughLine: The red line, a literal drawn line running down the page margin for the entire exhibit. It begins at the title as a thin black surveyor's ink line (1832, the plat), runs through every room as both timeline spine and scroll progress, turns permanently to HOLC D-grade red at the exact moment the federal letterhead appears in Act 5, thickens past the ledger entries it passes, and terminates in the final room at the visitor's own catalog card, under their own feet, in 2026. It is paired with a second, quieter system, the brass roman numerals I through V minted on the plinths in Act 3 and posted as signage at each downstream room, so the visitor always knows which instrument of the machine is operating. Together the line and the numerals make the owner's demand physical, elements that build off each other and carry the timeline into the present day.
title: The Paper Machine
visitorTakeaway: A week later the visitor remembers two physical sensations and one sentence. The drawer, that they pulled a real scanned sheet out of the dark and chose to see the typed line about their block. The climb, that their own thumb had to scroll six screens to get from the Black median to the white one. And the sentence the whole room was built to leave behind, that none of this was weather. Five documents did it, clerks filed them, public money paid for them, and the grade typed in 1940 is still under somebody's feet, possibly theirs.
